title: Verity Trail Watch
description: Ray Sabo's month-by-month record of the Verity Branch Trail being built on the old Marchfield and Coyne Flats branch line, from the first survey stakes in 2012 to the trailhead sign board in 2014.

data.author: Ray Sabo
data.tagline: Eleven and a bit miles of old railroad, being turned into a path. Photographed from the same two places every time.
data.about:
My name is [b]Ray Sabo[/b] and I live in Ashkettle. I ran the materials shed for the Verity County highway department from 1979 until I took the buyout in 2003, which means I spent twenty-four years finding out what rock and gravel actually were before the county put them under a road.

This site is one thing: [b]the Verity Branch Trail being built[/b], out of the old Marchfield and Coyne Flats branch line, from the first survey stakes in 2012 to whatever counts as finished. Eleven point two miles, Marchfield to Coyne Flats, crushed limestone, county parks department.

I walk it, I photograph it from the same two places every time, I measure what I can reach with a tape, and I write down the station numbers. Where I am guessing I say so. Where somebody who was there tells me I have it wrong, the correction goes under their name and my mistake stays where it was, which is the only way any of this is worth reading in twenty years.

I am not a railroad man, I am not an engineer, and I have no position on whether this should have been a trail. It is a trail. This is what happened to it.

My other site, about a road cut on Route 62, is [url=synth://quarrycut.net/]quarrycut.net[/url]. People write to me there about the radio and I have nothing to tell them, and I have even less to tell them here.

blogroll.label: The quarry cut on Route 62 -- my other page, in frames, not about this
Coyne Flats Community Association -- the depot page is the best thing on this line
Verity Rail enthusiasts' forum -- quiet since 2009, still up
Verity Rail Company, Marchfield Subdivision abandonment
T. Norris, surveyor -- the 1994 flood pages
Arndt Group, Bowes City -- the consultant (not answering)
County parks trail page (moved, I do not know where to)

posts.title: Starting this
posts.body:
I have had a page about the road cut on Route 62 since 2004. It is in frames, I typed it in Notepad, and the guestbook on it has been full of pharmacy advertisements since February 2010. The password went to an address at a company that stopped existing in 2006, and no part of that sentence has a fix in it.

So this is somewhere else. My nephew set it up in an afternoon on [url=synth://gridfallhost.net/]Gridfall Host[/url], seven dollars a month, and the name was nineteen for the year. The one thing it does that the other page does not is let me delete an advertisement.

[b]What it is for.[/b] The county owns the old Marchfield and Coyne Flats branch and has since 2011. The rail came out in 2009 and the ties went with it, and since then it has been eleven and a half miles of ballast growing box elder. There is going to be a path on it. A consultant has been walking it since January and there are stakes in the ground at the Marchfield end.

I am going to walk it and photograph it and write down what I measure, about once a month, until it is finished.

[img:photo:vtw-2012-03-17-freighthouse-north]

[i]The freight house from the north, 17 March 2012, ten past eight. This is one of the two places I will stand every time. The other is the south bank at Coyne Creek. The building is 1911 and the west end has been open to the weather since the 2004 storm.[/i]

[b]Rules, before I break them.[/b]

[list][*]Photograph from the same places. One picture of a thing is worth very little. Two from the same spot two years apart are worth a great deal and cost the same.[*]Put the date in the file name. All of them. I have three shoe boxes at home that prove why.[*]Measure rather than guess, and say what I measured it with.[*]When somebody who was there tells me I have it wrong, print the correction under their name and leave my mistake where it was.[/list]

I am not a railroad man. I ran the materials shed for the county highway department from 1979 until I took the buyout in 2003, which means I spent twenty-four years being paid to find out what rock and gravel actually were before somebody put them under a road. This job is about to be almost entirely gravel, so I am better placed than I deserve to be.

comments.author: A. Pitts
comments.body:
Mr. Sabo, this is Arlen Pitts, secretary of the Verity Rail Preservation Society. We have the 1918 valuation map for this line, sheets 6 through 11, and they give you the stationing, every structure, and the right of way widths parcel by parcel. You are welcome to photocopy them.

Second Tuesday, seven o'clock, Community Room B at the library, side door after six. [url=synth://verityrail-preservation.org/]Our site[/url] has not changed since 2009 and Kyle is at work.

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body:
Put the instrument in the caption, not at the bottom of the page. You did that eventually on the other site and it is why the other site is worth reading.

A tape is a tape. A wheel on ballast is out by more than people think.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: Good, somebody is doing this. Is it going to be paved? I have heard paved from two people and stone from one.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Crushed limestone, four inches, eight feet wide. Paving eleven miles costs about six times what this county has.

posts.title: The stakes are in as far as the Quarry Road crossing
posts.body:
There are stakes from the freight house lot out to Sta 158+40, which is the Quarry Road crossing, and then nothing. That is the end of the first design segment and not the end of anybody's interest.

[b]The stationing.[/b] The drawings call the Marchfield end 0+00 and the Coyne Flats end 591+36. A station is a hundred feet, so that is 59,136 feet, which is 11.2 miles. The signs will be in miles because nobody outside a survey crew thinks in stations. I will write both.

[b]What the lath means[/b], because people keep pulling them up.

[list][*]Pink lath in pairs out at the fence line: the edge of the right of way. Nothing gets built there. They are telling the contractor where the county's ground stops.[*]White lath with the station on it in keel: centreline, offset 25 feet left, which means the real centreline is 25 feet to your right as you face up-station. The offset is written on the lath. Read it.[*]Blue-topped hubs, a stub of two-by-two driven flush with a guard lath beside it: grade. The hub is the number. The lath is only so the dozer sees it.[*]"C 1.4" or "F 0.6" on a lath: cut one foot four, or fill six tenths, at that hub.[/list]

[img:photo:vtw-2012-04-21-lath-sta-104]

[i]Lath at Sta 104+00, looking up-station. The keel is faded on the south side of every one of them and sharp on the north, which is sun, and which is why a crew re-marks lath in the spring.[/i]

[b]What is under the path.[/b] I dug three holes with a spade in the ditch line, not the crown, because I did not want to be the man who put a hole in it. Sta 62+00, twenty-one inches of ballast over a sandy subgrade. Sta 118+00, seventeen. Sta 151+00, fourteen, and wet at the bottom.

The ballast is one-and-a-half inch crushed limestone, angular, in good shape below the top four inches. The top four inches is fouled with fines, leaf mould and a mat of roots, which is normal for three years of nothing and is what the grader is for.

A railroad ballast section is a better subbase than most roads in this county start with.

comments.author: dmc_marchfield
comments.body: the pink ones by the fence behind our place have been out twice now and it isnt me. somebody thinks theyre markers for a house

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: They are markers. They are just not for a house. If they come out again leave them lying rather than putting them back, because a lath in the wrong hole is worse than no lath, and ring the parks office with the station number off the one next to it.

comments.author: Kyle Stanek
comments.body: Clearest thing anyone has written about our line since the forum stopped. I will put a link on the Society page next time I am in it, which I am aware is a thing I have said before.

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body: Your three holes are three holes. They are not a sample and you have not called them one, which I note because most people would have.

posts.title: How the county came to own it, in the order it happened
posts.body:
Two mornings at the clerk's office and ninety cents in copies.

[list][*][b]14 March 2008.[/b] Last revenue freight. Three loaded cars of corn off the elevator east of Marchfield. It did not come down to Coyne Flats and that has not stopped anybody saying it did.[*][b]September 2008.[/b] Abandonment made final.[*][b]October 2008.[/b] The crossing gates came out at Quarry Road and at Kestrel Road, both crossings, one crew, two days.[*][b]Spring 2009.[/b] Rail lifted and sold by weight, ties out behind it. What is in the ground now is ballast and whatever fell off.[*][b]June 2011.[/b] The railroad conveyed the corridor to the county. Quitclaim, book 611 page 204, recorded 14 June 2011, one dollar and other valuable consideration. Nine pages of parcel description, two of which recite a fence that has not been there since 1974.[/list]

The county bought three strips outright where the original conveyance had run out or had never been clean. The largest is at Sta 290+00 and cost $2,400. That is the whole land cost of this trail.

[b]One thing worth saying.[/b] If you look up Verity Rail on [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/verity-rail]the county wiki[/url] you get the Gridfall branch, which is eighteen miles, ran to the quarry, and closed in March 2007. That is a different line with a different history, and about half of what people tell me about "the line" turns out to be about that one. The article is right. It is just not about this.

Ours is the Marchfield and Coyne Flats branch. Half the Society calls it the Cutler branch because of the cement plant and their own minutes use both names in one paragraph. The railroad's own page has the abandonment written out: [url=synth://verityrail.org/abandonment]verityrail.org, Marchfield Subdivision[/url].

comments.author: kfennimore
comments.body:
The conveyance was noticed in the Ledger of 22 June 2011, page 6, four column inches, under a headline calling it the Coyne Flats spur. It was never a spur. It had an agency, a timetable and a station, and a spur is a stub of track behind a building.

The library has the reel. I am on the reference desk Tuesday to Friday.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Thank you. I will come in. I have been told four times that this was a spur and I had nowhere to point people.

comments.author: A. Pitts
comments.body: The fence recited at Sta 380 is the old Deeter line fence, which came down when the farm was split. It is recited because the 1903 deed recited it and every deed since has copied the one before it, which is how a fence outlives a farm on paper.

posts.title: The four structures, and what is wrong with the fourth one
posts.body:
Four bridge structures in eleven miles. Three are short and nobody will think about them again. The fourth is the one every conversation about this trail is going to be about.

[b]Sta 89+76, mile 1.7 -- the farm crossing at Deeter's.[/b] A steel deck span of 30 feet over a lane that runs under the line. Dry stone abutments with concrete caps, and the caps are dated 1954 in the wet concrete at the north end, done with a stick.

[b]Sta 269+28, mile 5.1 -- Bracken Lane.[/b] Two riveted plate girders, 52 feet, over the road. A builder's plate on the west girder reads 1921. The tallest thing on the trail and the only place you will look down at traffic.

[b]Sta 337+92, mile 6.4 -- the culvert.[/b] Two structures stacked and hardly anybody knows it. Underneath is a dry stone arch culvert with a date cut into the south headwall. I have read it as 1889 twice and as 1869 once, and the once was in flat light, and I am not going to pick between them on this page. Over the top of it, on new concrete seats, is a 38-foot steel deck span that went in after the approach washed. The stone is still there and is now holding up nothing at all.

Everybody calls it the Kestrel Road culvert. Kestrel Road is two and a quarter miles back at Sta 216+48. The section gang called it that and the name stuck to the structure and not the place.

[img:photo:vtw-2012-06-23-culvert-headwall-south]

[i]The south headwall at 337+92, 23 June 2012, about four in the afternoon. The date is in the third course up, left of centre, with the tape extended to twelve inches lying on the stone, which is the only reason anybody can argue with me about it.[/i]

[b]Sta 427+68, mile 8.1 -- Coyne Creek.[/b] Timber pile trestle, 22 bents, over water. I put a tape on the south approach and got 214 feet 6 inches between back walls. The 1918 valuation map says 214, so I have stopped measuring it.

The county highway department inspected it on 16 August 1988. Two pages. It notes scour at what it calls pier 2 and recommends monitoring. There are no piers on that bridge. There are bents. The man wrote pier because the form said pier, and bent 2 is the one standing in water at normal flow.

I have not found an inspection between 1988 and now, and I have asked in two offices. That does not mean there was not one.

comments.author: D. Kilmartin
comments.body:
Dorothy Kilmartin, Coyne Flats, for the Society. Your 214 is right and it is sheet 10.

A-006 in our archive is the 1994 flood damage survey of the Coyne Creek approach and it is the only thing anybody has between 1988 and now. Four pages, and it is about the approach fill and not the bridge, so it will help you less than you want it to. You are welcome to it.

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body: Bent 2 from which end. Say which end. The 1988 report does not, and that is the reason it is a useless report, and not the reason people think it is.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Numbered from the south, which is how sheet 10 numbers them and how the 1988 report appears to, and I say appears because you are right that it does not state it.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: So they deck Coyne Creek like the other three and it is fine. It is a bridge, it is standing up, put boards on it.

posts.title: The grant, in the order the forms go
posts.body:
People keep telling me this trail is free money from the state. It is not free, and it is not from the state until about ninety days after the county has already spent it. The parks office gave me the whole file for nothing in eight days, so here it is.

[b]The application.[/b] Form SP-19, thirty-one pages plus mapping, a resolution of the county board, and a letter from the highway department undertaking to supply the match in labour. The county applied in the 2011 round and did not get it: scored 62 of 100, and the line fell at 71. The 2012 application is the same document with the scoring narrative rewritten and a page of support letters added, and it was funded.

[b]The award.[/b] $248,000. Eighty-twenty, so the county's match is $62,000, of which $41,000 is highway hours, equipment and haulage valued at the state's own rates and $21,000 is cash out of the parks capital line. Total project as written, $310,000.

[b]Where it goes.[/b] Design and permitting $34,000, and inside that the four-bridge structural assessment is $18,400. Clearing and earthwork $96,000. Surface course $61,000. Bridge decking and rail $28,000. Signage, gates, bollards and the trailhead $54,000. Contingency $37,000.

[b]Getting paid.[/b] Form SP-44, quarterly, in arrears, certified payrolls and every invoice attached. The county pays the contractor out of its own money and then asks for it back. The first claim went in on 1 October, came back on the 19th for a missing signature page, went again, and the money landed eleven weeks after the work it paid for.

[b]The condition at the back.[/b] The county must keep it open to the public as a trail for twenty-five years or repay with interest. That is page two of the award letter, and it is why nobody at the county will ever say out loud that a piece of this trail might close.

At the public meeting in September, thirty-one people asked about dogs, horses, quads, liability, toilets and the trestle, in that order. Nobody asked what it would cost to keep it once it was built. I did not either. I am writing that down so I remember I did not.

comments.author: A. Pitts
comments.body: Eight days and no charge is better than the Society has ever had out of that office, and I do the asking. Which office, and whose name.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Parks, second floor of the annex, and I asked in person on a Wednesday morning instead of writing. That may be the whole trick.

comments.author: FEDERAL GRANT PARTNERS
comments.body: Municipalities and non-profits! You may be eligible for UNCLAIMED recreation funding in your area. No cost eligibility review, we are paid only on award. Limited slots this cycle. [url=synth://grant-award-check.top/verity]Free eligibility check here[/url]

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: First one of those. I said this site would let me delete them and I have left this one so I can point at it later.

comments.author: Bev Stanek
comments.body: Twenty-five years. Our own fund has sat at $14,212.40 since November 2007 and I redraw the thermometer every year to say the same thing. Twenty-five years is not long to a county and it is very long to a treasurer.

posts.title: The bridge assessment came, and it is 84 pages
posts.body:
[b]Structural Assessment, Four Bridge Structures, Former Verity Rail Branch.[/b] Rennert Engineering, Marchfield. March 2013. Eighty-four pages. $18,400 out of the design line.

It is not with the clerk. It is with the records custodian at Public Works, a different office in a different building, and the form is VC-114. I am writing that down because it took me two wrong tries and somebody after me should not have to.

[b]The three short ones.[/b] Deeter's, Bracken Lane and the culvert span all come back sound for pedestrian loading with a timber deck bolted to the existing steel. Some rivets at Bracken Lane, paint everywhere, and the abutment cap at Deeter's wants pointing. That is the whole of it for three bridges.

[b]Coyne Creek.[/b] Pages 38 to 44.

[list][*]Section loss in the stringers throughout. Not in one place. Throughout.[*]Bent-by-bent table on page 41. Fourteen of the twenty-two bents recommended for replacement.[*]Scour at the two bents standing in water, which is what the county wrote down on 16 August 1988 and recommended monitoring.[*]Classed not suitable for pedestrian loading in its present condition.[*]Page 44 gives two options and there are only two. Replacement in kind, or removal.[/list]

There is no third option on that page where you lay boards on it. I read page 44 twice looking for one.

There is also [b]no cost figure anywhere in the document[/b]. I went through it a second time for that alone. An assessment is not an estimate and this one does not pretend to be, but the consequence is that the county now has a report telling it to do one of two things and no paper at all saying what either costs.

I am a man reading an engineer's report and I am not an engineer. What I can tell you is what the pages say and which page they say it on.

[img:photo:vtw-2013-04-06-assessment-p41]

[i]Page 41, the bent table, photographed on my kitchen table because the copier at the library eats the shading in the right-hand column, and the shading is which ones are bad.[/i]

comments.author: D. Kilmartin
comments.body: The Society has asked for a copy and been told $12.75. We will pay it. Fourteen of twenty-two is worse than anything anybody here has said out loud.

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body: Section loss throughout is the sentence. Not the fourteen bents. A bent can be replaced by anybody with a crane and a chequebook. Stringers running the whole length is the bridge.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: Still say deck it. Every one of these reports says the worst thing it can say. That is what they are for.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: That is a fair thing to believe and I believed it in June. Form VC-114 at Public Works, and it is not free, and I would rather you read the pages than take my word.

comments.author: c_pruitt
comments.body: Ten years late, but I have just requested this on Form VC-114 on the strength of this page. Nobody at the county told me which office had it and nothing published since 2014 says so either.

posts.title: What they did with the ballast
posts.body:
Trewin Construction of Bowes City had notice to proceed on 13 May and they are at Sta 341+00. This is the part I actually know something about, so it is the long one.

[b]They did not take it away.[/b] People keep asking me where the ballast went. It went about eight feet sideways.

The top three to four inches of it is fouled -- fines, leaf mould, roots, thirty years of the woods getting in. A grader took that off in two passes and windrowed it on the shoulders. It is sitting there in two low ridges either side of the path and it will be sitting there in fifty years. Underneath is clean angular one-and-a-half inch limestone, sixteen to twenty inches of it, and that is the subbase. Nobody bought it, nobody hauled it, and it is better than what is under most of the roads in this county.

Shaped with a grader, watered, rolled with a padfoot and then a smooth drum. Two per cent crown, which means the middle is an inch and a half higher than the edges on an eight-foot path, which you cannot see and which is the entire reason it will not be a puddle.

[b]Four soft spots.[/b] Undercut, geotextile and eight inches of number two stone in three of them: Sta 352+00, Sta 401+00, Sta 476+00, all places where the fill crosses a swale and the ditch above has silted in.

The fourth is Sta 214+00 to 219+00, the wet ground at Kestrel Road, and they could not fix that one because there is nowhere for the water to go. So there will be a boardwalk: 180 feet, six-by-six sills on helical piles, two-by-eight deck, southern yellow pine, by Hollick Brothers of Kerrin.

I told the foreman it will be ice end to end in January, because timber holds frost hours after stone has come good. He said he knew that and that it was not his to decide. I believe both halves of that.

[b]The surface course.[/b] County spec: three-eighths inch minus crushed limestone, eight to twelve per cent passing the number 200, compacted four inches. I wrote the grandfather of that specification in about 1994 with two other men. The eight to twelve is the part that matters. Under eight and it will not bind and you are walking on marbles. Over twelve and it turns to grease in April.

[b]Two things came out of the ditch this month.[/b] A cast iron whistle post at Sta 101+00, W on the face, broken at the base, which went back in the ditch where it was. And twenty-two feet of rail at Sta 131+50 the 2009 salvage crew either missed or did not think worth the lift, 85-pound section, rolled 1926 by the brand on the web.

[img:photo:vtw-2013-07-20-windrow-sta-341]

[i]The fouled ballast windrow on the north shoulder at Sta 341+00, 20 July 2013. My boot is in the shot for scale, size eleven, which is the kind of photographer I am.[/i]

comments.author: wpennock
comments.body: Eight to twelve passing the 200 is a number a stranger can check the work against, which is more than the county has published anywhere about this job.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: So the crunchy stuff at the edges is the old railroad ballast and the smooth stuff in the middle is new. I have walked past that for weeks thinking the edges were where they had been sloppy.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: That is it exactly, and it is not sloppy, it is deliberate and it is free.

comments.author: M. Ferro
comments.body: 85 pound and 1926 is right for that end. Everything east of the culvert was 90 pound relaid later. Ferro, and I was one of the forty people stood at Quarry Road in 2008 and I have the tripod to prove it.

comments.body: B-e-s-t p-r-i-c-e for garden and outdoor tool, big catalog, fast ship 3 day. [url=synth://outdoor-deals-mega.click/catalog]view our catalog[/url]

posts.title: A date nail, and the four pads at Sta 369+60
posts.body:
Two things at the same station, so one entry.

[b]The nail.[/b] A date nail is a nail with the year stamped in raised figures on the head, two digits, driven into a crosstie so the road can tell how old the tie is without keeping a book. You walk a line counting heads and you know what you have. Most roads stopped using them by about 1970.

This one is steel, round shank, two and a half inches, head seven-sixteenths across, with a raised [b]44[/b] under sixty years of rust. 1944.

It was on the fouled ballast windrow on the north side at Sta 369+60, mile 7.0, sitting on the surface where the grader put it a fortnight ago. Not buried. People picture digging. The rail and ties went out in 2009 and the nails went with the ties, and what is loose now got dropped, kicked or bladed and lies in the cinders under leaf litter. You find them by walking with your eyes down.

[img:photo:vtw-2013-08-24-datenail-44-on-tape]

[i]The nail on the tailgate with the tape under it, 24 August 2013. The 4s are sharp on the left and worn on the right, which is the side that took the hammer.[/i]

I put it back. The railroad's own site says the company left these on the ground deliberately and has no objection to anybody picking one up now the land is not theirs. The county's park ordinance says the ditch and the cinders are the park and that taking something off the surface of a park is removal. Both of those are about this nail and neither office has spoken to the other about it. I telephoned parks and was told the man who would know was out.

So it is back on the windrow at 369+60, head up. Somebody will find it again.

Tom Norris walked two miles of this alignment with a tripod in 2007, found a 1951 one and left it where it was, and there is a minute and a half of that on [url=synth://clipvault.tv/]ClipVault[/url] with no narration on it at all. His page is [url=synth://tnorris.verity.net/]here[/url].

[b]The pads.[/b] Four concrete pads in a line off the north side at the same station, each about the size of a kitchen table, with rusted bolts standing out of them. They are the mill siding: Hazlett and Son, feed and grain, at Nye Mills. The siding came out sometime in the seventies -- I have been told 1973 and 1976 by two men who were both there and I am not going to arbitrate that. The building came down in 1989.

[list][*]Two pads 38 by 54 inches, 26 feet apart, four one-inch bolts each on a thirty-inch square. The legs of the loading dock canopy.[*]One pad 44 by 44 with six bolts in two rows, sheared flush on four. The feed hoist.[*]One pad 30 by 30 with no bolts left and a square hole cast in the middle. I do not know what this one is and neither does anybody I have asked.[/list]

There is no picnic table here and there never was one. I say that in advance because the pads look exactly like what somebody would put a picnic table on, and I have heard it twice this summer.

Arlen Pitts sent me the 1961 annotation on valuation sheet 10, which gives the siding at 340 feet with the words FEED MILL in a hand that is not the draughtsman's.

comments.author: A. Pitts
comments.body:
44 is right for that end. The branch was re-tied in 1943 and 1944 under the wartime programme and the Society has the superintendent's letter asking for the timber, A-021, two pages, mostly about not getting it.

1951 is right for the Halsey end. They did that segment in two seasons and the nails run 51 and 52 mixed.

comments.author: g_hazlett
comments.body:
My grandfather ran that mill until 1968. The hoist was electric from 1952 and a gasoline engine before it, and the engine sat in a shed on the far side that is not in any picture I have seen.

There was a scale set into the dock floor about fifteen feet north of the big pad. I would like to know whether the pit is still down there.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: I am not going to dig on county ground. I put a length of rebar down in four places about where you say and hit stone at eleven inches in one of them and nothing in the other three. That is all I can honestly give you.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: You put the nail back? I would have had it on the shelf by Sunday lunch and I am not sure that is wrong.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: It may not be. I had a telephone call that did not get answered, and putting it back is what you do when you do not know.

posts.title: Decking the Bracken Lane span
posts.body:
All three of the short bridges get their decks between 30 September and 8 November. Bracken Lane took longest and it is the one people will stand on.

Nothing structural was done to it. The steel was already carrying itself and had been since 1921.

[list][*]Wire brushed and spot primed where the paint had gone, which was most of the top flange and the whole north end.[*]Six-by-eight treated sleepers across the top flanges at two-foot centres, drilled and bolted through with three-quarter inch galvanised bolts. Ninety-four holes, drilled on site, by a man on his knees with a magnetic drill.[*]Three-inch treated running plank on the sleepers, laid tight, ends staggered.[*]Pipe rail both sides, 42 inches to the top rail, welded posts on clips bolted to the girder web.[/list]

[b]The handrail is the whole story of this job.[/b] The grant requires 42 inches. The drawing set showed 36. Nobody caught it until the posts were fabricated. The change order was $1,900 and three weeks, on a contract of $310,000, and it is the most expensive six inches on this trail.

Eleven working days, three men. Materials for all three bridges came to $23,600 and Bracken Lane is $9,240 of it.

[img:photo:vtw-2013-10-26-bracken-lane-deck]

[i]Bracken Lane from the road, 26 October 2013. Rail up, plank down. The 1921 plate is on the west girder just left of the third post, which you cannot read in this picture and which I have photographed separately.[/i]

Nobody has been to Coyne Creek. There is nothing in this contract about Coyne Creek and I have read the contract.

posts.title: The winter, and the fence at Coyne Creek
posts.body:
Work stopped on 20 December and started again Monday. Four below on the 28th of January, and the limestone stockpile at the Marchfield end froze into one piece the size of a shed.

The fence went up at Coyne Creek in the week of 3 February. Six-foot chain link across both ends of the trestle, driven posts set in the ballast, a gate in the north fence for inspection access with a county padlock on it, and a sign wired to each: white on blue, [b]BRIDGE CLOSED -- STRUCTURE UNDER EVALUATION -- VERITY COUNTY PARKS AND RECREATION[/b].

Under evaluation. The evaluation was delivered in March 2013, it is eighty-four pages, and I have read it.

[img:photo:vtw-2014-02-22-coyne-creek-fence-north]

[i]The north fence, 22 February 2014, about nine in the morning, from the south bank spot I have used since March 2012. The creek is frozen in this one, which it has been three times in three winters.[/i]

[b]One measurement.[/b] The gap between the end post of the north fence and the face of the abutment is twenty-six inches. I put a tape on it. That is enough for a person to get round the end without touching the fence and without any effort at all.

I am not saying anybody has. I am saying I measured twenty-six inches on the 22nd of February and that it is written down here with the date on it.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: Twenty-six inches. Somebody is round that by June.

I have started photographing this fence every autumn and I have three now. Yours from February 2014 is the earliest picture of it that exists as far as I can find, and the sign in it is the same sign with more paint on it.

Is there any chance of a copy. I will pay the postage. F. Wardlow, Marchfield.

posts.title: Limestone
posts.body:
Three thousand one hundred tons of three-eighths minus crushed limestone out of the pit at Ardo, $11.40 a ton delivered. $35,340 of an item budgeted at $61,000 with the placing in it.

Forty-one loads a week at the peak. Sarles and Son of Coyne Flats had four trucks on it and there were two owner-operators besides, and one of those put a load in the ditch at the Kestrel Road approach on a Tuesday and everybody was very kind about it.

Spread in one lift with a box on a skid steer, watered from a tanker, rolled with a three-ton double drum. Eight feet wide with a foot of shoulder either side. Four inches compacted, about five and a half loose, and you can see the difference behind the roller if you stand in the right place.

[b]The county tested it.[/b] Density every five hundred feet and a gradation on every fourth day's delivery. I asked for the sheets and got them. The gradations run between nine and eleven per cent passing the 200, which is inside the spec and is where you want to be in it. That is a good job by whoever was loading at Ardo and I would like it written down somewhere, so it is written down here.

[img:photo:vtw-2014-04-05-surface-behind-roller]

[i]Behind the roller at Sta 233+00, 5 April 2014. The line across the middle is where Friday morning's work stopped and the afternoon's started, and in two months you will not find it.[/i]

One thing that will go wrong. The approach up to Kestrel Road runs at 1.9 per cent for about four hundred feet, which is the steepest grade on this whole railroad and tells you everything about what railroads are. Water will run down it and take fines with it, and that four hundred feet will want topping up every three or four years. Somebody should write that in a book. I do not think anybody is going to.

comments.author: g_reitz
comments.body: What tyre will this take? I have 28s and everybody on the internet says 38s for stone.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Rolled three-eighths minus with eleven per cent fines in it is not gravel, it packs nearly hard. You will be fine on 28s except in the first fortnight and after heavy rain. I am a man with a spade and not a bicycle man, so take that for what it is.

posts.title: They took the freight house down on Tuesday
posts.body:
Tuesday 22 April. A tracked excavator with a thumb, two men and a flagger. It started at twenty to eight, the end wall was off by about ten, it was down and in a pile by two, and the pile was gone by Thursday.

The Marchfield freight house went up in 1911 and was the last railroad building standing in Verity County. Granite came into it by rail for the monument works until 1989. The roof over the west end had been open to the weather since the 2004 storm and there was a bird's nest in the office ceiling with a second one built on top of it.

[b]The salvage.[/b] The Society were let in on the 15th and 16th with a list and a deadline. They came out with the sliding door, nine feet of door track and two hangers, the platform scale plate out of the freight room floor, a coffee tin of square nails, and the stencil off the inside of the freight room wall reading VERITY RAIL CO -- MARCHFIELD, which came away in three pieces because it was painted on the boards and not on paper. Arlen Pitts stood at the fence on the Tuesday from about half past seven. Roy Tibbets did not come.

[b]The caboose.[/b] VR 4412 went on a lowboy on Thursday 27 March to the county fairgrounds at Gridfall, where the fair board has given it a pad by the north gate. The move cost $3,900 out of the Freight House Fund, which had stood at $14,212.40 since November 2007 and now stands at $10,312.40. The Society's own page still shows the old figure, because the man who edits it has a job.

[img:photo:vtw-2014-04-22-freighthouse-endwall]

[i]22 April 2014, about ten past ten, from the road, which is where I was told to stand. Three other people were photographing from the same stretch of shoulder, one of them out of the passenger window of a car stuck behind the contractor's truck that could not get past.[/i]

[b]I did not know this building.[/b] I have been inside it twice, both times in the last two years, both times to photograph the floor. My father did not work for the railroad and nobody in my family did. I went out on Tuesday because somebody ought to have a photograph of the north elevation with a date on it, and now there are eleven of them.

The Ledger ran it Thursday, page 3, four paragraphs and a picture of the machine.

[b]What goes there.[/b] The lot gets finished in the autumn and parks has a shelter on the drawing: twelve by twenty, six posts, steel roof, concrete floor, going in about forty feet south of where the building stood. Where the building stood is going to be the third row of parking.

comments.author: A. Pitts
comments.body: For the record, because somebody will ask in twenty years and we will not be here: we asked for sixty days on 9 January and were refused in writing on 3 February, and the letter says no further extension will be granted. That is the fourth ask and the first refusal. The previous three were granted and we did nothing with any of them. That is in our minutes and I put it there.

posts.title: They cut the ribbon on Saturday
posts.body:
Saturday 17 May, ten o'clock, at the Marchfield lot. I counted 146 people and then everybody moved and I gave up.

Commissioner Paul Renko spoke for four minutes and was the best of them. Curt Haldeman from parks spoke for nine. A young man from the state representative's office read a letter for two minutes and handed the letter to Haldeman, who put it in his coat. The chamber president spoke, briefly, mostly about parking. The scissors came from the parks office and would not cut the ribbon, and a man in the second row had a pocket knife.

[b]The numbers said out loud.[/b] Eleven point two miles. Three hundred and ten thousand dollars. Two years.

The 11.2 is right: the county's own stationing says 591+36, which is 11.2 miles to within nine feet. The $310,000 is right if you count the in-kind match, which nobody in the crowd would have known was in the number. Two years is right if you start at the 2012 application. The first public notice about a footpath on this line went up at Marchfield in June 2006, and the plastic wallet it was in had already gone cloudy.

Nobody said the words Coyne Creek.

[img:photo:vtw-2014-05-17-ribbon]

[i]Ten past ten, 17 May 2014. The ribbon is already cut in this one because I was photographing the new milepost at 0+00, which is my own fault entirely.[/i]

[b]Then I walked it.[/b] Marchfield to the fence is 8.1 miles, three hours five minutes with stops. Then I drove round by Kestrel Road and Sarles Road to the Coyne Flats end and walked the other 3.1 up to the far fence, an hour and ten. That is the whole trail, and the whole trail cannot be walked in one go and will not be for as long as that fence is there.

Two things from the far end, which gets a tenth of the traffic and is the better half. There is standing water across the full width at Sta 454+08, mile 8.6, four inches deep and twenty feet long in the third week of May, because the ditch on the north side is blocked by the new shoulder windrow. And there is still railroad in the ground at both approaches to the trestle: twenty-two feet of rail on the north approach, still spiked to about sixty feet of ties, with new limestone laid up against it and over the tie ends. The salvage crew stopped at the bridge in 2009 because you cannot get a machine onto a bridge like that, and nobody has been back.

The county parked an ambulance at the lot for the morning and it was used twice before lunch. That is in somebody else's log: [url=synth://scanner.verity.net/post/log-2014-05-17]the scanner log for 17 May[/url].

comments.author: D. Kilmartin
comments.body:
Nobody from Coyne Flats spoke and nobody from Coyne Flats was asked to. Eleven and a half miles of this ran to our end and the ribbon was at the other one, which is where the car park is, which is where it was always going to be. I am not bitter. I would have liked to be asked.

Our end is written up properly here: [url=synth://coyneflats.org/depot]The Depot[/url].

posts.title: The lot, the shelter, and the map on the board
posts.body:
The permanent work at the Marchfield end went in during October, five months after the ribbon.

[list][*][b]The lot.[/b] Fourteen spaces, one marked accessible, gravel with a bituminous apron where it meets the road. $21,400.[*][b]The shelter.[/b] Twelve by twenty, six posts, green steel roof, concrete floor, about forty feet south of where the freight house stood. Delivered on a truck in three pieces and stood up on Tuesday 14 October in most of a day. $6,800.[*][b]Bollards.[/b] Removable, county padlock, one at the Quarry Road crossing and one at Kestrel Road. $410 each.[*][b]The sign board.[/b] Four feet by six, two posts, plexiglass front on a hinge, $2,850, printed by a vendor in another state.[/list]

[img:photo:vtw-2014-11-08-sign-board]

[i]The board on 8 November 2014. Photographed square on with the sun behind me, which took three visits, because that plexiglass will show you the car park and not the map at any other angle.[/i]

[b]The map on it is the 2013 design drawing.[/b]

It shows the route running continuously from the Marchfield lot to the Coyne Flats lot. It crosses Coyne Creek on the trestle. There is no break in the line, no hatching, no note, and nothing anywhere on the board to say that the bridge at mile 8.1 is fenced at both ends and has been since February.

The fence was up eight weeks before that map went to the printer. I have a photograph of the fence dated 22 February and the purchase order for the board is dated 18 April.

I wrote to the parks office on Monday 20 October, one page, with the station number on it. I had an acknowledgement on Monday 27 October saying the request had been forwarded to the appropriate department. Nothing since.

It is a label and a roll of tape. I have said so twice and I will say it once more in writing in the spring.

People are going to ride out of that lot expecting eleven miles because the board tells them eleven miles, and get eight and a fence. I watched two groups turn round at it in one afternoon in September.

comments.author: trailhound
comments.body: Watched a family turn round at that fence last Sunday and the man was furious, and he was furious at the fence and not at the map.

comments.author: g_reitz
comments.body: Ask them for the vendor's name and ask the vendor what a replacement panel costs. It is usually a smaller number than anybody at a county expects and it ends the argument.

comments.author: Ray Sabo
comments.body: Good idea and I will do it.

comments.author: c_pruitt
comments.body: Eight years on and the board still shows the 2013 alignment. It has faded now, which is going to solve it in the end.

posts.title: That is the trail
posts.body:
I started this in March 2012 to write down what happened to eleven and a bit miles of old railroad while it was being turned into a path, once a month, with the dates on the photographs. The path is built. So this is the last one.

[b]What it came to.[/b]

[list][*]11.2 miles. Sta 0+00 at Marchfield to Sta 591+36 at the Coyne Flats freight house field.[*]$310,000, of which $248,000 was the state grant and $62,000 the county's match, and $41,000 of that match was hours and equipment rather than money.[*]3,100 tons of three-eighths minus limestone at $11.40 delivered.[*]Three bridges decked between 30 September and 8 November 2013. One fenced at both ends since the week of 3 February 2014.[*]One building down, 22 April 2014. One caboose moved nine miles to a fairground.[*]2,140 photographs, every one with the date in the file name, on two drives and a spindle of discs in a cake tin at my sister's.[/list]

[b]What is still wrong, as of this morning.[/b]

[list][*]The map on the trailhead board shows a route across a bridge that has been fenced since February.[*]Standing water at Sta 454+08 every spring, because the ditch is blocked by the shoulder windrow.[*]The boardwalk at Kestrel Road will be ice in January. It was in January. It will be again.[*]Twenty-six inches between the north fence post and the abutment at Coyne Creek.[*]No marker of any kind where the freight house stood. I have asked twice.[/list]

None of those is a disaster and all five are a morning's work for two men.

[b]Why I am stopping.[/b] A path that is finished does not need a man writing down what happened to it every month. I would rather the last entry be about the trail than have six years of entries about a sign board.

If the county ever does the trestle I will come back and photograph it, and I will start at the south bank where I have stood every time since 17 March 2012.

[img:photo:vtw-2014-12-20-south-bank-last]

[i]The south bank spot, 20 December 2014, twenty past eight. The thirty-first photograph from this exact place. Frost on the fence and the sign starting to go at the top corner.[/i]

Anybody who wants copies, write to me. The postal address is on [url=synth://quarrycut.net/]my other page[/url] and has not changed since 1977. I am not putting an address in a box on the internet again, and if you want to know why, look at the guestbook on that page and count the real messages.

I am leaving this up. It is seven dollars a month at [url=synth://gridfallhost.net/]Gridfall Host[/url] and it is on the card, and a card that keeps working is how most things stay up.

The Society has printed the whole of this site on the library copier at four cents a page and it is in the cabinet as A-047. Sixty-one pages.

That is not a compliment about your writing. It is that you are the only person who wrote any of it down while it was happening.
